title: How would you estimate how many smartphones are sold in India each year?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How many smartphones are sold in India each year?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: India buys roughly 150 to 175 million new smartphones a year. A simple estimate gets there in three steps: 1.4 billion people, about half with a smartphone, each replaced every four years, which gives about 175 million. In a population this large, the ownership rate and the replacement cycle do almost all the work, so those are the two numbers to defend. Try your own estimate before you read on.
body:
The question

How many smartphones are sold in India each year?

Large populations punish loose assumptions. Moving the replacement cycle by one year changes the answer by tens of millions of phones. The interviewer wants to see you pick sensible inputs, segment where it matters and check yourself against reality.

Clarify before you calculate

  • New phones only? Assume yes. Second-hand and refurbished phones are a large market in India but a separate one.
  • Units or value? Units, per year.
  • Sold to whom? Phones bought by consumers. Industry trackers count shipments into shops, which can differ from sales in any one year because of stock building.

Rough guess: "A bit over a hundred million. India is one of the largest phone markets in the world."

Step by step

  1. People in India: 1.4B.
  2. Share who own a smartphone: 50% → 1.4B × 50% = 700M owners. This excludes young children, many older people and those who still use basic feature phones.
  3. Years before an owner replaces the phone: 4 → 700M ÷ 4 = 175M phones a year.

That is close to 480,000 phones a day (175M ÷ 365), which sounds plausible for a country of 1.4 billion people.

Sanity check from a second angle

Ownership and replacement both differ sharply between cities and villages, so check the estimate by segment. Assume roughly 36% of Indians live in urban areas:

SegmentOwnersReplaced everyPhones a year
Urban500M people × 75% = 375M3 years125M
Rural900M people × 35% = 315M5 years63M

That gives 690M owners, about the same as before, and 125M + 63M = 188M phones a year. Both methods land between 175M and 190M.

Check against reality

IDC reports that India shipped about 152 million smartphones in 2025, roughly flat on 2024. Our estimates are 15% to 25% high. Work backwards to see why: if 700M owners bought 152M new phones, the implied replacement cycle is 700M ÷ 152M = about 4.6 years, not 4. Second-hand and refurbished phones also absorb some replacement demand. That is a useful thing to say out loud: the check tells you which assumption to revise.

Which assumption matters most

The replacement cycle. At five years instead of four, replacements fall from 175M to 700M ÷ 5 = 140M, a drop of 20%. The ownership share is second: every 10 percentage points of ownership is 140M owners, or 35M phones a year on a four-year cycle.

A complete model adds two flows the shortcut ignores:

  • First-time buyers, as more people move from feature phones to smartphones. This adds to demand.
  • Second-hand purchases, which meet some demand without a new phone being sold. This subtracts.

New phones sold = replacements + first-time buyers − demand met by used phones. In India these two corrections partly offset each other, which is why the simple model is a reasonable start.

What a strong answer sounds like

"I'll size this as a replacement market. Of 1.4 billion people, about half have a smartphone, so 700 million owners. If they replace every four years, that's about 175 million phones a year. Splitting urban and rural gives about 190 million. Trackers put shipments nearer 150 million, which suggests the real replacement cycle is closer to four and a half years, or that used phones take a share. The cycle is the assumption that moves this most."

A weak answer multiplies 1.4 billion by an ownership rate and stops there, which confuses the number of phones in use (a stock) with the number sold each year (a flow).

Common mistakes

  • Stock versus flow. 700M phones in use is not 700M phones sold. Divide by the replacement cycle.
  • One rate for a whole subcontinent. Urban and rural India behave very differently. Segmenting takes a minute and makes the answer more credible.
  • Ignoring used phones. In price-sensitive markets, a meaningful share of "replacements" are second-hand.

Practice

1. Roughly what is the Indian smartphone market worth in a year?

Show the answer

IDC put the average selling price at about $282 in 2025. Using our 175M phones × $280 = about $49B. On the reported 152M shipments, it is about $43B.

2. Apple shipped about 14M iPhones in India in 2025, according to IDC. If iPhone owners replace every three years, roughly what share of Indian smartphone owners use an iPhone?

Show the answer

Work from flow to stock: 14M a year × 3 years = about 42M iPhones in use. 42M ÷ 700M owners = about 6%. The same stock-and-flow logic, run in reverse.

Where to practise next

Replacement cycles drive UK car tyres and UK student laptops too. Read the numbers worth knowing for the population anchors, and for a full telecoms case with a market twist, try Sunrise Mobile, about a mobile operator whose subscribers grow while revenue shrinks.
